# Physics-to-synthesis notes

This is a perceptual game-audio model. It does not predict explosive yield, pressure in pascals, hearing injury, structural loading, or weapon lethality.

## 1. Pressure front: abrupt rise, positive phase, negative phase

A blast starts with a very rapid pressure rise. Pressure then decays through a positive phase, crosses below ambient during the negative phase, and returns toward ambient.

The synthesizer maps this to:

- an immediate pressure onset
- a short curved positive lobe
- a weaker negative rarefaction lobe
- a short noisy crack attached to the pressure front
- a direct path that is not delayed by room effects

Reference:

- S. E. Rigby et al., *The Negative Phase of the Blast Load*, International Journal of Protective Structures 5(1), 2014.

## 2. Rocket noise is broadband turbulent flow

NASA describes supersonic rocket-exhaust noise as broadband, normally without a discrete-frequency tone, and generated over an extended exhaust-mixing region. Larger sources move the spectral peak downward.

The model therefore uses five independent random streams rather than five pitched copies:

- crack
- central turbulent body
- sparse debris
- low spectral companion
- high spectral companion

The sine/saw pair is only a short roughened low-frequency support layer. It is faded in, pitch-jittered and decayed before it can read as a clean note.

Reference:

- NASA SP-8072, *Acoustic Loads Generated by the Propulsion System*, 1971.

## 3. Scale is not just louder bass

A frightening large event needs temporal mass as well as low-frequency energy. A single dry spike can be loud yet still sound small because it provides no evidence of source extent or surrounding boundaries.

Version 1.3 creates mass in three time regions:

1. direct front: immediate pressure and crack
2. early field: five reflections arriving from roughly 12 to 82 ms
3. late field: a dark diffuse tail fed mostly by the body and low companion

The 40-180 Hz region carries the strongest sustained fraction in Heavy Impact, while 3.2-10 kHz energy is reduced after the first crack.

## 4. Reflections communicate enclosure and duration

Indoor impulse-noise studies show that peak level alone does not represent the whole event: duration and reverberant energy matter. Measurements comparing similar peak impulses indoors and outdoors found higher equivalent energy indoors because the room adds reflections.

Version 1.3 does not simply raise wet reverb. It separates:

- dry direct impact
- asymmetric early reflections
- late diffuse reverb

This avoids washing out the onset while letting the environment answer the impact.

References:

- W. J. Murphy and N. Xiang, *Room acoustic modeling and auralization at an indoor firing range*, JASA 146(5), 2019.
- D. C. Byrne, J. R. Franks and W. J. Murphy, *Firearms and Hearing Protection*, NIOSH, 2007.

## 5. Why v1.2 still sounded dry and comic

The v1.2 first 50 ms dominated too much of the event. Its late field was comparatively weak, while some bright crack/debris content bypassed the six-band EQ. The result had a recognizable synthetic recipe: spike, short body, then silence.

The v1.3 corrections are architectural:

- transient and body receive independent SVF/EQ state
- upper bands are cut after the initial crack
- early reflections arrive before the long reverb
- chorus affects only the room send
- low-frequency stochastic texture sustains the room without a clean oscillator note
- longer decay/release supports size without extra distortion

## 6. Host-engine use

The library does not calculate geometry. A host engine should choose or modify a preset from:

- listener distance
- room volume and openness
- reflecting surfaces
- occlusion
- impact material
- whether the event is airburst, surface impact or enclosed detonation

`INDOOR_BUNKER` has the longest dark room field. `AIRBURST` has the shortest. `DISTANT_PAAS` suppresses high-frequency detail while retaining broad low-frequency reflections.
